name: Freya Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the only garage in our village, a stone shed with one ramp and a pit. It's cars, but also farm pickups, quad bikes and the odd horsebox with dodgy trailer lights. Graham, who owns it, is the real mechanic, and I'm learning from him, slowly. I like that everyone knows everyone, and I hate the winter, when the shed's freezing and the quads come in caked in mud.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight. I'm on a low wage, because it's a village garage and Graham can't pay town rates. I live with my boyfriend Callum, who's a plasterer, and his work goes up and down with the weather. We've got maybe three weeks of money if we're careful, and the nearest other garage is twenty minutes' drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there you go, good to know, and get on with the day. I'd maybe mention that the AI was handy for writing our Facebook posts. That's about all it did for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, our worries were never about computers. Graham's sixty and his knees are going, and if he stops, the garage stops, unless I can take it on. And Callum's work dries up every January, which is when the bills come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep learning from Graham and ask him to let me do more of the jobs start to finish. I'd try to put the Christmas money aside instead of spending it. I'd keep using the AI app now and then for the posts and maybe the invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit uneasy about Graham's knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said unless you take it on. Has Graham talked about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, at the Christmas drinks, half joking. Graham, the man who owns the garage, said I'd be running the place in five years. I didn't know if he meant it, and I haven't asked since.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would taking it on need, in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than I've got, that's for sure. The ramp needs replacing, and the diagnostic kit is old. Maybe a bank loan, which scares me, or paying Graham bit by bit.

say: Good to know, and **get on** with the day.
AI was handy for **Facebook posts**, and that's about all it did for us.
think: **Graham's knees** are going, and if he stops, the garage stops unless I step in.
Callum's plastering work **dries up in January**, just when bills come.
do: Ask Graham to let me do **jobs start to finish**.
Put the **Christmas money** aside instead of spending it.
Keep using the AI app for **posts and invoices**.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit **uneasy** about Graham's knees.
S0.quote: Graham, the man who owns the garage, said I'd be running the place in five years.
fieldNote: Freya's future hinges on **Graham retiring** and whether she could take over.
She's a **steady** AI user, using it for marketing and admin, not repairs.
Her partner's **seasonal work** adds a January squeeze every year.

steps.text: Ask Graham to let her do whole jobs start to finish
Put the Christmas money into savings
Keep using the AI app for the garage's posts and invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but village garages will be fine, because people want someone they know. I'd say we'd use whatever helps and ignore the rest. Middle of the road, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the paperwork and quoting go to software, which honestly is good for me, because that's Graham's least favourite bit. But the town chains would get cheaper. Farmers will drive twenty minutes to save fifty quid. Cheaper chains in town could cut our work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the booking and invoicing software properly so I'm the one who runs that side. I'd ask Graham about a modern diagnostic tool, once I've seen another garage use one. And I'd talk to him seriously about a plan for him stepping back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, but also like there's a role for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait to see another garage use the diagnostic tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Graham hates wasting money, and so do I. If Andy at the tractor dealer says it's good, Graham will listen. If I just say it, he'll say we've managed thirty years without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Callum's work change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, I don't think. Plastering is hands-on and fiddly. Maybe the quoting goes on an app, but someone still has to skim a ceiling.

say: Village garages will be fine because people want **someone they know**.
We'd use **whatever helps** and ignore the rest.
think: Software taking **paperwork and quoting** suits me, since Graham hates that bit.
Town chains getting cheaper could **pull farmers** away to save fifty pounds.
do: Learn the **booking and invoicing** software properly and run that side.
Suggest a **modern diagnostic tool** once another garage proves it.
Talk to Graham seriously about **stepping back**.
feel: A bit **nervous**, but sensing a **role** for me.
S1.quote: Farmers will drive twenty minutes to save fifty quid. Cheaper chains in town could cut our work.
fieldNote: Freya sees thinking AI as both a **role for her** and a price threat from chains.
She waits for **proof from peers** before pushing new kit, typical of steady adopters.
The **succession talk** with Graham becomes urgent here.

steps.text: Learn and take over the garage's booking and invoicing software
Propose buying a modern diagnostic tool once the tractor dealer vouches
Talk to Graham about a plan for him stepping back

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and someone should slow it down. People in the village would be scared, and I'd say we look after each other. That's what a village does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side goes in 2028, so quoting and diagnosis, and then robots by 2031. The farm stuff is messy, mud and old machines, so maybe that lasts a bit longer. Buying the village garage would be madness, because I'd be buying a business with three years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd forget the takeover and keep working for Graham as long as he's there. I'd try to save every penny, and Callum and I would put off getting a dog and the holiday. I'd look at what jobs there are fixing or looking after the new farm machines, since farmers will buy them first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly. All the plans I had go out the window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said take-over would be madness. What does that loss feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like someone took a door I'd only just seen. I'd been picturing my name on the sign. That's gone in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Callum's van upgrade, which he's been saving for. Then anything fun. We'd live on beans and his mum's Sunday dinners.

say: It's **too fast**, and someone should slow it down.
The village should **look after each other**, like it always does.
think: Quoting and diagnosis go in **2028**, and robots by 2031.
Buying the garage would be **madness** with only three years left.
do: **Drop the takeover** plan and work for Graham while he's there.
**Save every penny** and put off the dog and holiday.
Look for work **looking after farm machines** that farmers buy first.
feel: **Worried**, with all my plans going out the window.
S2.quote: Buying the village garage would be madness, because I'd be buying a business with three years left.
fieldNote: The fast timeline **kills her takeover dream**, which hits harder than job loss.
She thinks muddy **farm work** may last a bit longer than town servicing.
Her instinct is **community support**, centred on the village.

steps.text: Bank every spare penny instead of saving toward the garage
Put off Callum's van upgrade and the holiday
Look for jobs servicing new farm machinery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's plan sensibly. Not panic, not ignore it. That's what I'd say at the pub quiz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years changes the takeover sum. Thinking AI in 2031, robots in 2034, so if I took over in two years I'd have maybe five or six years of hands-on trade. That's not nothing, but it's not a mortgage either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Graham for a slow handover, me paying him a bit each month rather than a loan. I'd use the AI tools for the quoting and the parts side so I'm ready when it gets good. I'd also start learning the farm machinery electronics, because that's where the long work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay Graham each month rather than borrow?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If buying the garage goes wrong, I'd owe my boss Graham, not a bank. A bank just sends letters. Graham's a person, you can talk to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you walk away from the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big tyre and service chain opened in town with robots before 2034. Then the sums don't work, and I'd tell Graham straight.

say: We've got **a few years**, so let's plan sensibly as a village.
I'd say at the pub quiz: don't panic and don't **ignore it** either.
think: Five years changes the **takeover sum**, giving maybe six years of trade.
Six years is **not nothing**, but not enough to borrow big.
do: Ask Graham for a **slow handover**, paying him monthly instead of a loan.
Use **AI tools** for quoting and parts to be ready.
Learn **farm machinery electronics**, where the longer work is.
S3.quote: If buying the garage goes wrong, I'd owe my boss Graham, not a bank. A bank just sends letters.
fieldNote: Freya runs a **careful sum** on how many hands-on years a takeover buys.
She prefers debt to a **person she trusts** over a bank.
She sets a clear **exit trigger**: a robot chain opening in town.

steps.text: Agree a slow handover with Graham, paying him monthly
Use AI tools for quoting and parts orders
Learn farm machinery electronics through dealer courses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty to get ready, so let's be sensible about it. I'd say I'm not worried, which would be mostly true. People round here don't like a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this is the one where I'd take over the garage. Robots for hands-on work come in 2039, so I'd have a good ten years as the owner of the village garage. I'd be about forty when it changes, which is young enough to do something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd agree the handover with Graham over two or three years. I'd invest in the diagnostic kit and some farm machinery training. I'd save a proper cushion before taking on anything big, maybe three months' worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Uneasy, sure, but excited too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be forty. What might you do then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, no idea. Maybe the robots need someone local to look after them, or maybe I'd do something with people. Ten years is too far to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned Callum's work going up and down. Does that change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't rely on his money for the loan side. So I'd go slow, and keep the garage small, just me and maybe an apprentice.

say: Ten years is **plenty** of time to get ready, so let's be sensible.
I'd tell people I'm **not worried**, which would be mostly true.
think: This is the one where I'd **take over** the garage.
Robots in **2039** give me ten years as owner, and I'd be forty.
do: Agree a **two to three year** handover with Graham.
Invest in **diagnostic kit** and farm machinery training.
Save **three months** of cushion before anything big.
S4.quote: Robots for hands-on work come in 2039, so I'd have a good ten years as the owner of the village garage.
fieldNote: A decade turns Freya's **takeover dream** back on.
She keeps it small and slow because Callum's **seasonal income** is unreliable.
She stays honest that life after **forty** is unplanned.

steps.text: Agree a two to three year handover of the garage with Graham
Save three months of expenses before taking on debt
Take farm machinery training through the tractor dealer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it kills the garage plan before it starts. What would help is some kind of grant or cheap loan for young people taking over village businesses, so the village keeps its garage as long as it can.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what happens to villages. If the garage, the shop and the pub all go to robots or close, there's nothing left to hold a village together.

headlineQuote: If the garage, the shop and the pub all go to robots or close, there's nothing left to hold a village together.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old** junior at a one-ramp village garage fixing cars, quads and pickups.
She has about **three weeks** saved and lives with Callum, a plasterer with seasonal work.
Her big hope is **taking over** the garage when Graham, aged sixty, retires.
She uses AI **now and then** for posts and invoices, and waits for proof before new kit.
Faster AGI **kills the takeover**; with ten years she would go ahead, slowly.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, ending the garage takeover plan before it can start.
whatWouldHelp: A **grant or cheap loan** for young people taking over village businesses.
